clinicalPearls: Refers to progressive growth of a corticotroph pituitary tumour after bilateral adrenalectomy performed for Cushing disease
Loss of cortisol negative feedback allows the residual corticotroph adenoma to enlarge and secrete large amounts of adrenocorticotrophic hormone
Very high circulating adrenocorticotrophic hormone drives striking skin hyperpigmentation
An expanding sellar mass can cause headache, visual field defects and hypopituitarism
Risk is greater in younger patients and when adrenalectomy is done without pituitary irradiation
Regular monitoring of adrenocorticotrophic hormone levels and pituitary imaging after bilateral adrenalectomy allows early detection
Prophylactic pituitary radiotherapy at the time of adrenalectomy reduces the likelihood of later tumour progression
Management centres on transsphenoidal surgery, with radiotherapy and medical therapy for residual or aggressive disease
reference.pathophysiology: Nelson syndrome develops when a corticotroph adenoma, previously the source of Cushing disease, continues to grow after the adrenal glands are surgically removed. With cortisol production abolished, the normal suppressive feedback on the pituitary is lost, unleashing the tumour to proliferate and to secrete high levels of adrenocorticotrophic hormone and its related pro-opiomelanocortin peptides. The excess melanocyte-stimulating activity of these peptides produces marked hyperpigmentation, while the enlarging adenoma exerts local mass effect on adjacent structures. A subset behave aggressively with invasive growth.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent or persistent Cushing disease before adrenalectomy
Primary adrenal insufficiency hyperpigmentation without tumour progression
additionalInvestigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to assess tumour size and invasion
Anterior pituitary hormone profile to detect hypopituitarism
Assessment of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement adequacy
Histological and proliferative characterisation of resected tumour
redFlags: Rapid visual field loss from chiasmal compression
New hypopituitarism from an enlarging mass
Very high and rising adrenocorticotrophic hormone with worsening pigmentation
Adrenal crisis from inadequate replacement during tumour-related stress
reference.prognosis: Early detection and effective transsphenoidal resection, with adjuvant radiotherapy where needed, give a reasonable outlook, but aggressive corticotroph tumours can be difficult to control and cause significant morbidity through mass effect and hypopituitarism.
pitfalls: Failing to monitor adrenocorticotrophic hormone and pituitary imaging after bilateral adrenalectomy
Attributing hyperpigmentation solely to adrenal insufficiency without checking for tumour progression
Delaying intervention until visual compromise occurs
Not considering prophylactic pituitary radiotherapy in high-risk patients
Overlooking new anterior pituitary deficiencies from the enlarging adenoma
management: Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the corticotroph adenoma as the primary treatment
Adjuvant pituitary radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery for residual or aggressive tumour
Medical therapy to control ACTH secretion and tumour growth, such as pasireotide, cabergoline or temozolomide for aggressive disease
Optimisation of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement following bilateral adrenalectomy
Replacement of deficient anterior pituitary hormones and monitoring of visual fields for chiasmal compression
Surveillance with serial plasma ACTH measurement and pituitary MRI for early detection of tumour growth
Management through an endocrinology and pituitary neurosurgery multidisciplinary team
